passage:
Vandana hovered near the kho-kho game, hands behind her back. She almost said, "Can I play?" and then did not.
The boy called Darshan, dodging past, glanced at her. "Vandana! We need one more!"
"Me?"
"Yes, you. Sit in that row, and when I tap your back, run."
"What if I'm slow?"
"Everyone's slow the first time. Come on."
She sat down. On the third tap she ran and was caught almost at once. She laughed anyway, and the whole team groaned, and someone made room for her at the end of the line.

qa.q: Which game were the children playing?
qa.a: They were playing kho-kho.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling while she stood by the game with her hands behind her back?
qa.a: She felt shy and exposed. She wanted to ask to play but could not bring herself to say it.

qa.q: What small step by Darshan changed Vandana's afternoon?
qa.a: He noticed her, invited her by name and told her exactly what to do, so joining felt easy.

qa.q: What might Darshan have noticed about Vandana before he called her?
qa.a: He may have noticed her hovering with hands behind her back and thought the team could use one more player.

grounding: A child waiting at the edge of a game is invited in by a friendly peer.

passage:
My name is Maria, and there was a ball game in the colony park that afternoon. I stood at the edge with my hands in my pockets, waiting for someone to say, "You can play." Nobody did. My face went hot, as if everyone could see me waiting.
I told myself I didn't want to play anyway and began walking toward the gate.
Preeti Didi, sitting on the steps with a notebook, called, "Maria, come and keep score for me. I can't count and bat." I sat beside her, and after a while somebody threw me the ball.

qa.q: Where was the ball game?
qa.a: It was in the colony park.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling as the narrator waited at the edge?
qa.a: Maria felt exposed and small, with a hot face, and then told a comforting story about not wanting to play.

qa.q: What choice could Maria have made at the edge of the game?
qa.a: Maria could have asked, 'Can I join?' or chosen to sit near someone friendly instead of walking away alone.

qa.q: What might Preeti Didi have noticed to call Maria over?
qa.a: Preeti Didi may have seen Maria waiting and then heading for the gate, and found a small job that made room for Maria.

grounding: A child waits to be asked into a game, drifts away, and a friendly older girl changes the afternoon.

passage:
Playground note, Class 3, Monday.
At lunch break Baljeet stood by the fence for fifteen minutes watching the kho-kho game. Twice he took a step forward when a team was short, then stepped back. He kept twisting the strap of his water bottle. Nobody looked his way.
I didn't want to force it, so I asked Karan, the captain, "Your team looks one short. Anyone you'd pick?" Karan looked around and called, "Baljeet! Come, you're with us."
Baljeet ran in so fast he nearly tripped. Later he was sitting with Karan at lunch.
Next step: rotate captains, and keep an eye on the fence.
Sarita

qa.q: Which game was Baljeet watching?
qa.a: The kho-kho game.

qa.q: What does Baljeet twisting his bottle strap suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt nervous and exposed, wanting to join but unsure he'd be welcome.

qa.q: What did Sarita do that helped without forcing it?
qa.a: Sarita asked the captain, Karan, whether anyone could fill the gap, so the invitation came from a peer.

qa.q: How did things change between Karan and Baljeet?
qa.a: Karan went from not noticing Baljeet to picking him, and later they sat together at lunch.

grounding: Shows a child waiting at the edge of a game feeling exposed, and an adult quietly prompting a peer to invite him.

passage:
Thursday
New school, third week. At break the others play football near the water tank and I always stand at the side kicking a stone. My stomach feels tight and I pretend I'm looking at something far away.
Today I told myself, just ask. I walked up to Thomas, who sits in my row, and said, "Can I play?" My voice came out tiny. He said, "Sure, you're goalie." I let in four goals!! But I saved one and Thomas said "nice" 🙂
Tomorrow I'm going to ask again. Maybe not as goalie.
Uday

qa.q: What position did Thomas give Uday?
qa.a: Goalie.

qa.q: How was Uday feeling while standing at the side?
qa.a: Uday felt nervous and left out, stomach tight, pretending to look at something far away.

qa.q: What brave step did Uday take, and what could help next time?
qa.a: Uday walked up and asked, "Can I play?"; asking again early, before teams form, could make it easier.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Thomas to be asked?
qa.a: Thomas seemed to find it easy to say yes, and his "nice" after the save helped Uday feel welcome.

grounding: Shows a child at the edge of a game feeling exposed and small, then bravely inviting themselves in.

passage:
At the village fair ground near the canal, the older children were flying kites, shouting and tugging. Rafiq stood at the edge with his hands in his pockets. He had no kite. Nobody asked him to hold a spool. After a while he turned and began walking home along the dusty path, kicking at dry grass.
Tejas, whose kite had just tangled, saw him go. "Rafiq! Wait! I need someone to hold the spool while I fix this."
Rafiq turned slowly. "Me?"
"Who else? Come on."
By sunset Rafiq was running along the canal with the string cutting into his fingers, laughing, while Tejas shouted directions.

qa.q: What did Tejas need help with?
qa.a: Someone to hold the spool while the tangled kite was fixed.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling as he walked home?
qa.a: Rafiq felt left out and small, with no kite and nobody asking, so he drifted away.

qa.q: What small thing made the difference for Rafiq?
qa.a: Tejas noticed him leaving and gave him a real job, holding the spool, which pulled him into the game.

qa.q: What would change if Tejas hadn't looked up?
qa.a: Rafiq would have walked home alone, likely feeling even more shut out, instead of laughing by the canal at sunset.

grounding: Shows a child at the edge of a game drifting away until a peer notices and gives him a way in.

passage:
At the London primary school, the lunchtime football game was already going when Bao came out. He stood at the edge of the pitch, hands in his pockets, ball-watching. Nobody looked at him. He shifted from foot to foot. He didn't know whether to ask. What if they said no, in front of everyone?
After a few minutes he turned towards the benches.
Kofi, who was in goal, saw him go. "Hey! Bao! We need one more on the red team. You in?"
Bao turned back. "Me?"
"Yeah, you. You're on Musa's side. Go!"
Bao ran on. Two minutes later he passed the ball to Musa, who scored. Musa high-fived him.
At the bell, Kofi shouted, "Tomorrow, Bao. Same team."

qa.q: Who invited Bao to join the game?
qa.a: Kofi, who was in goal, saw him and invited him.

qa.q: What was Bao worried about as he stood at the edge?
qa.a: Bao felt nervous and exposed, worried that the others would say no in front of everyone.

qa.q: What made the difference to Bao's afternoon?
qa.a: Kofi noticed Bao drifting away and called him in by name, turning an awkward wait into being part of the team.

qa.q: What might Kofi have been feeling when he saw Bao turn away?
qa.a: Kofi likely felt kind and a bit concerned, noticing Bao was left out and wanting to include him.

grounding: A child standing at the edge of a game feels exposed and starts drifting away, and a friendly peer noticing changes the afternoon.
